content: However, selecting antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens that are compatible with TB treatment remains challenging due to drug interactions, such as those between rifampicin and lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or nevirapine (NVP). The 2013 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs recommend triple-nucleoside therapy for children based on evidence from randomized controlled trials. For children on LPV/r-based regimens who require rifampicin-based TB treatment, adding ritonavir (RTV) to achieve a 1:1 ratio with LPV is supported by interim pharmacokinetic studies, though final analyses are needed to confirm these findings. Broader guidance on co-treatment regimens for HIV and TB is also provided. Recommended ART Regimens for Children on TB Treatment: 1. Children under 3 years old: Triple NRTI therapy (zidovudine [AZT] + lamivudine [3TC] + abacavir [ABC]) is recommended during TB treatment. 2. Children 3 years and older: Two NRTIs plus efavirenz (EFV) or triple NRTI therapy can be used. For children already on ART when starting TB treatment: Children under 3 years on NNRTI-based regimens (e.g., NVP): Continue NVP with an adjusted dose (200 mg/m²) or switch to triple NRTI therapy. Children 3 years and older on NNRTI-based regimens: If on EFV, continue the same regimen. If on NVP, substitute with EFV or triple NRTI therapy. Children on PI-based regimens (e.g., LPV/r): For those under 3 years, either switch to triple NRTI therapy or continue LPV/r with added RTV to achieve full therapeutic dosing. For children 3 years and older, EFV substitution is preferred if there is no history of NNRTI regimen failure. If there is a history of failure, triple NRTI therapy or LPV/r with added RTV is recommended. Infant Prophylaxis: ART should be initiated urgently in all pregnant and breastfeeding women, even if identified late in pregnancy or postpartum, to reduce maternal viral load and prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission. Infants born to mothers with HIV at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with AZT (twice daily) and NVP (once daily) for the first 6 weeks of life, regardless of feeding method. Breastfed infants at high risk should continue prophylaxis for an additional 6 weeks (total of 12 weeks) using either AZT and NVP or NVP alone. High-Risk Infants: High-risk infants are defined as those born to mothers with: Less than 4 weeks of ART before delivery. A viral load >1,000 copies/mL within 4 weeks before delivery. Incident HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding. HIV first identified postpartum. Breastfeeding Recommendations: In settings where breastfeeding is promoted, mothers with HIV should exclusively breastfeed for the first 6 months, introduce complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for 12 months while on ART. Breastfeeding should only stop when a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. For HIV-infected infants, extended breastfeeding is recommended for as long as feasible. Research Gaps: Further studies are needed to: Assess ART adherence and retention in care among breastfeeding mothers. Investigate the impact of prolonged infant prophylaxis on resistance and toxicity. Develop improved ARV formulations, such as fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) suitable for infants. Implementation Considerations: Operational challenges include identifying high-risk infants, ensuring timely administration of prophylaxis, and addressing maternal ART adherence. Simplified dosing regimens and the development of dispersible FDC tablets for infant prophylaxis are priorities to improve feasibility and acceptability.
